name: Generating Assessments
title: Generating Assessments
answer: Generating assessments covers the creation of test items, question banks, rubrics, distractors, and formative checks aligned to learning objectives. It spans multiple choice, short answer, scenario based, and performance tasks across disciplines. The work supports instructors who need varied, standards aligned material without starting from a blank page. It also includes adapting existing items for accessibility, reading level, or alternate versions.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Generating assessments covers the creation of test items, question banks, rubrics, distractors, and formative checks aligned to learning objectives. It spans multiple choice, short answer, scenario based, and performance tasks across disciplines. The work supports instructors who need varied, standards aligned material without starting from a blank page. It also includes adapting existing items for accessibility, reading level, or alternate versions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most current systems run on hosted large language models accessed through APIs, often with a retrieval layer that pulls from course syllabi, textbooks, or item banks. Some institutions run smaller open weight models on local servers to keep student data inside their own network. The output typically flows into a learning management system or a question bank format such as QTI. Compute needs are modest at generation time because the models are pre trained.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical workflow begins with the instructor supplying learning objectives, source material, and constraints such as grade level, item type, and number of questions. The model generates candidate items, then a separate pass checks alignment, factual accuracy, and distractor plausibility. Many practitioners use a human in the loop review, editing or discarding items before they reach students. Some systems use structured prompting or few shot examples to keep the style consistent with an existing exam.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on who owns generated items, whether source material was licensed for this use, and whether student data is exposed to a third party model. There are also concerns about bias in item wording, cultural assumptions in scenarios, and the possibility that generated questions test surface recall rather than deeper understanding. Provenance matters because an item bank may mix human written and machine generated content, and later audits need to know which is which. Institutions often set rules about disclosure, review, and retention.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward assessments that adapt to a learner's demonstrated level and generate follow up questions or hints in real time. More work is going into automatic item analysis, where the system flags questions that performed poorly or showed unexpected patterns across groups. There is also interest in generating performance tasks and rubrics for project based work, not just discrete test items. Over time, the boundary between generating an assessment and generating feedback during learning is likely to blur.
